intro: The Steele lab works with bacteria associated with the bactivorous soil amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum to investigate the evolution of predation resistance, virulence, and symbiosis. We combine molecular biology and microbiology techniques with comparative genomics, phylogenetics, transcriptomics, and transposon mutagenesis to understand the molecular mechanisms underlying host-microbe interactions.
modelSystemText: D. discoideum has been used for decades to study chemotaxis, cell differentiation, development, the virulence mechanisms of human pathogens, and the evolution of altruism. In its natural ecological role, it is both a voracious generalist predator and a host for a variety of intracellular pathogenic bacteria. By identifying the genes bacteria use to interact with D. discoideum, we can trace the evolutionary path that determines whether a microbe becomes a symbiont or a pathogen.
strategiesText: We focus on two bacterial genera that associate with D. discoideum in nature and represent two different strategies for handling predation: free-living Pseudomonas, and facultatively endosymbiotic Paraburkholderia.

projects.title: GacA and predation resistance
projects.text: Characterizing the role the transcription factor GacA plays in predation resistance across multiple Pseudomonas lineages.

projects.title: Cooperation, cheating, and survival
projects.text: Measuring how cooperation and cheating within Pseudomonas populations affect their ability to resist predation.

projects.title: Surviving inside the phagosome
projects.text: Identifying the genes endosymbiotic Paraburkholderia need to survive inside the host phagosome, to understand the molecular mechanisms at work.

projects.title: Phagosome maturation and infection
projects.text: Investigating how Paraburkholderia infection changes phagosome maturation in Dictyostelium discoideum.
